title: Umair v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)
frame:
Forum: Federal Court.
Parties as styled: applicants = MOHAMMAD UMAIR NAZIA HAMNA UMAIR MOHAMMAD HUZAIFA SHEIKH MUHAMMAD HUSSAIN SHEIKH; respondent = THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): This application for judicial review is dismissed, because the Decision (as defined later in these Reasons) is reasonable and procedurally fair.
How the layers nest here: The judge is the author (layer 1). The applicant and respondent in this proceeding make submissions to the judge (layer 2). The decision under review was made by an earlier decision-maker (layer 3), and that decision may itself report what a claimant, the Minister or a witness said to that decision-maker (layer 4).

paragraphs.text: This is an application for judicial review of five decisions dated October 21, 2024, by an Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada [IRCC] officer [the Officer], rejecting the work permit application of the first-named Applicant, Mohammad Umair [the Principal Applicant], under the International Mobility Program [the Program], as well as the applications of the other Applicants, his wife and children as accompanying dependents [the Dependents].
This application for judicial review is dismissed, because the Decision (as defined later in these Reasons) is reasonable and procedurally fair.

The Applicants are citizens of Pakistan. The Principal Applicant works in the manufacturing industry and has incorporated a business in Ontario, said to specialize in producing lightweight building blocks for construction.

On June 4, 2024, the Principal Applicant submitted a work permit application under the Program for a period of one year. Applications were also submitted for the Dependents to join the Principal Applicant during his time in Canada. The record before the Court includes the documents submitted in support of those applications, including a Commitment Certificate issued by the so-called incubator under the Program [the Incubator], dated December 4, 2023, and expiring on June 4, 2023 [the Commitment Certificate].

On October 21, 2024, the Officer issued letters to each of the Applicants conveying the decision that their application had been refused. Each of the Applicants filled an application for leave and for judicial review of the decision refusing their application. By Order dated December 19, 2024, Justice McVeigh consolidated these applications under the present Court file number. For purposes of these Reasons, I will refer to the decisions on the Applicants’ applications collectively as the “Decision”.

The letter issued to the Principal Applicant stated that the Officer was not satisfied that he would leave Canada at the end of his stay as required by paragraph 179(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 [IRPR], based on: (a) his current employment situation not showing that he was financially established in his country of residence; (b) the compensation indicated in his job offer and his assets and financial situation being insufficient to support the stated purpose of travel; (c) his inability to demonstrate that he would be able to adequately perform the work he sought; (d) his lack of significant family ties outside Canada; and (e) his inability to adequately demonstrate that he met the requirements of the work permit he sought under section 205 of the IRPR.

The following entry in the Officer’s Global Case Management System [GCMS] notes also informs an understanding of the reasons for the Decision: I have reviewed the application. Application under A77. Family of five. I note on the IMM 5766 that the applicant and one other person are listed as essential. Applicant's valuation/chartered account document(s) reviewed. These documents will not be considered given that the report(s) are a paid for document/statement and do not include evidence of funds available that have not already been reviewed. Funds available at time of application unclear due to dated bank statement in comparison to date of application. Bank statements for both the applicant and business partner are dated in 2023. Applicant’s stated employment and education noted however there is no supporting documentation to support this. As a result I am not satisfied the applicant that the applicant will be able to adequately perform the proposed work. Applicant’s representative describes economic benefits to include the hiring of “manufacturing, sales, administration and management” positions and the commitment certificate indicates one of the urgent business reasons to be to “hire a Canadian team” yet I note the financial forecast for salaries in the supplied deck notes salary costs to be under 50K CAD for each of the first 5 years of business. Applicant has not satisfied me of the creation of significant economic or social benefit. Financials forecast for this type of business appear modest in the plan overall. Applicant’s commitment certificate was expired at time of application. Overall, applicant has not adequately demonstrated that he meets all of the requirements of A77. Weighing the factors in this application. I am not satisfied that the applicant will depart Canada at the end of the period authorized for their stay. For the reasons above, I have refused this application

The letter issued to each of the other Applicants stated that the Officer was not satisfied the Applicant would leave Canada at the end of their stay as required by paragraph 200(1)(b) of the IRPR, based on: (a) the Applicant not having significant family ties outside Canada; and (b) the purpose of their visit to Canada not being consistent with a temporary stay given the details provided in the application.
The Officer’s GCMS notes reflect reasons consist with those letters, as well as referencing the fact that the Principal Applicant’s application had been refused.

Based on the parties’ submissions, which concern the Officer’s reasons for the Decision as it relates to the Principal Applicant, the issues for the Court to determine in this application are: whether the Decision is reasonable on its merits; and whether the Officer deprived the Applicants of procedural fairness in arriving at the Decision.
paragraphs.heading_before: IV. Issues and Standard of Review

paragraphs.text: As is implicit in the articulation of the first issue, the merits of the Decision are reviewable on the standard of reasonableness, as informed by the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65.

The procedural fairness determination requires the Court to assess whether the procedure followed was fair having regard to all the circumstances (Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at para 54).

Rather than considering the parties’ arguments surrounding reasonableness and procedural fairness as two separate issues, it will be most efficient to structure these Reasons around the various bases for the Decision that the Applicants seek to impugn.

The GCMS notes demonstrate that the Officer’s reasons for the Decision include not being satisfied that the Principal Applicant would be able to adequately perform the proposed work. The Officer noted the Applicant’s stated employment and education but found that no supporting documentation had been provided. At the hearing of this application, the Applicants identified documents in the Principal Applicant’s work permit application that speak to these subjects.
paragraphs.heading_before: A. Ability to perform the proposed work

paragraphs.text: The Applicants argue that the Officer’s conclusion represents a concern with the authenticity of the Principal Applicant’s experience and qualifications and therefore a veiled credibility finding, imposing upon the Officer a procedural fairness obligation to advise the Principal Applicant of that concern and afford him an opportunity to address it before making the Decision.

The Respondent accepts that credibility concerns heighten the procedural fairness obligations owed to an applicant and give rise to a duty to provide an opportunity to address such concerns. However, the Respondent disagrees with the Applicants’ characterization of the Officer’s concerns with the Principal Applicant’s experience and qualifications as a credibility finding.

I agree with the Respondent’s characterization of the documents upon which the Applicants rely as representing self-descriptions by the Principal Applicant, and I further agree with the Respondent that the Officer’s concern in relation to those documents was with the sufficiency of this evidence. The GCMS notes do not demonstrate the Officer raising a credibility or authenticity concern. Rather, the concern was that the Principal Applicant failed to provide any sort of supporting documentation in relation to his stated employment or education. Visa officers are not required to inform applicants of concerns regarding the sufficiency of supporting materials or evidence (Mohamud v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 1140 [Mohamud] at para 14; Patel v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 77 at para 10).
I find no breach of procedural fairness in connection with this aspect of the Decision.

The GCMS notes further demonstrate that the Officer was not satisfied with the evidence provided in support of the Principal Applicant’s financial ability. The Officer states that the funds available at the time of application were unclear, because the bank statements were outdated compared to the date of the application.

Again, the Applicants submit that this conclusion represents a veiled credibility finding. I again disagree with this characterization of the Officer’s reasoning. I appreciate that, unlike the self-descriptions of education and experience canvassed above, the bank statements are documentation generated by a financial institution. However, the Officer’s concern was that the statements were not current and therefore were insufficient to demonstrate the Principal Applicant’s financial capacity.

In support of their argument, the Applicants note that the financial documentation submitted in support of the Principal Applicant’s application were the same as had been provided by the Incubator, and that the accompanying correspondence from the Principal Applicant’s representative to IRCC stated that, should IRCC require updated documents, it should not hesitate to send a request letter. This aspect of the record does not assist the Applicants. It was the Principal Applicant’s onus to provide sufficient documentation and, as noted above, the Officer had no obligation to inform the Principal Applicant of concerns as to the sufficiency of his submissions (Mohamud at para 14). The correspondence to IRCC does not alter that principle.

The Applicants raise similar concerns with respect to the Officer’s comments on the documentation from the Principal Applicant’s accountants. The GCMS notes state, “These documents will not be considered given that the report(s) are a paid for document/statement and do not include evidence of funds available that are not already been reviewed.” I agree with the Applicants that this statement by the Officer implies a concern about the credibility of the accountants’ documentation, based on the fact that the accountants are paid for their services. This is the sort of concern that could give rise to a procedural fairness obligation.

However, I accept the Respondent’s position that, in the matter at hand, the failure of the Officer to alert the Principal Applicant to this concern, and afford an opportunity to respond thereto, is not material to the Decision. As the Respondent notes (and consistent with the Officer’s statement), the information from the accountants, like the bank statements, dated to 2023 and therefore did not have the potential to cure the Officer’s concern that the information was not current.
Again, I find no breach of procedural fairness.

The Applicants note the statement in the Officer’s GCMS notes that the Commitment Certificate had expired at the time of application. The Applicants argue that this is factually inaccurate, as his application was submitted on June 4, 2024, the date of the Commitment Certificate’s expiry. The Respondent accepts this assertion. However, the parties disagree on the significance of the factual error.

The Applicants argue that the Officer’s error represents a significant misapprehension of the facts underlying the application, which undermines the reasonableness of the Decision. The Respondent takes the position that this error is not material, arguing that the Officer’s principal reasons for refusing the Principal Applicant’s work permit application were the sufficiency of evidence on available funds and the sufficiency of evidence establishing the Principal Applicant’s ability to perform the relevant work. The Respondent argues that either of these reasons is determinative of the outcome of the Decision.

I agree with the Respondent’s position that, on the facts of this case, the factual error with respect to the Commitment Certificate does not represent a reviewable error. It is not particularly clear from the GCMS notes whether the Officer considered what they misunderstood to be submission of the application after the expiry of the Commitment Certificate to be a determinative issue. However, even if the Decision were to be interpreted in that manner, I accept the Respondent’s position that the Officer’s reasoning with respect to availability of funds and ability to perform the relevant work are themselves determinative issues. As I have found no reviewable error in those aspects of the Officer’s reasoning, the factual error in relation to the Commitment Certificate does not undermine the reasonableness of the Decision.

Finally, the Officer noted that, because the Principal Applicant’s financial forecast for salaries was under $50,000 for each of the first five years of business, the Principal Applicant had not satisfied the Officer of the creation of significant economic or social benefits. This finding relates to paragraph 205(a) of the IRPR, which provides that a work permit may be issued to a foreign national who intends to perform work that would create or maintain significant social, cultural or economic benefits or opportunities for Canadian citizens or permanent residents.

In connection with this finding, the Applicants noted at the hearing of this application that the written submissions in support of the Principal Applicant’s work permit application referenced a variety of economic benefits, social benefits, and cultural benefits, which extended beyond the impacts of the salaries to be paid to Canadian workers. The Officer’s analysis does not reference these other categories of benefits.

I accept this point. However, as with the above analysis surrounding the Commitment Certificate, it remains the case that the Officer’s reasoning with respect to availability of funds and ability to perform the relevant work are themselves determinative issues. As such, because I have found no reviewable error in those aspects of the Officer’s reasoning, any shortcoming in the Officer’s benefits analysis does not undermine the reasonableness of the Decision overall.

For the foregoing reasons, this application for judicial review will be dismissed. Neither party proposed any question for certification for appeal, and none is stated. JUDGMENT IN IMM-19664-24 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that this application for judicial review is dismissed. No question is certified for appeal. "Richard F.
